u1: What impressed me most was how they handle authority, with the principle of mandar obedeciendo, or leading by obeying. Their representatives carry out what the assembly decided, and they stay answerable to the people who gave them the mandate.
u2: Most institutions pile up layers and offices as they get older. The Zapatistas reviewed theirs and moved authority down. They didn't write a book on leadership and start a certification program. They actually changed the system they were living in.
u3: They've warned people themselves not to import or export Zapatismo as a ready-made model. What's worth copying is how they learn. They build something and ask questions. They find out where the practice fails, and then they change the structure.
u4: They also don't prove my whole economic path, from unpriced internal necessities to a common purse to getting rid of outside money. Zapatista communities pool their work to support their schools and clinics, their autonomous government and their resistance. They also sell things and trade, and they get support from outside. What they do show is that major necessities and public functions can be taken off the market and run collectively. Outside help can build capability. But it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence, when the specialist, the donor or the organization stays indispensable.
u5:
To celebrate ten years of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened the Escuelita. Outsiders came to stay with families, and they learned autonomy by taking part in daily life there. About 1,500 students came to the first sessions, and thousands more came to the later ones.

One way an escuelita can fail is by turning into a visitor business. Then the residents spend their lives putting on a show of community for outsiders who pay, and success gets measured by how many guests come instead of how many daughter communities get started. It shouldn't be about making people feel transformed for a week. It should teach enough of the social and material system that some of them can build it somewhere else.
u6: I also tried, in my research, to trace what came out of the Escuelita. I found alumni networks and people taking practices home, and there was organizing later on. What I couldn't find was a clear line from someone attending the Escuelita to a newly founded communal institution, along with evidence of how that institution's members and their kids actually did over time. The Zapatistas were already influencing people internationally before the Escuelita existed, so a later resemblance doesn't prove it came from there. I'm borrowing their way of teaching and their ambition to replicate, without claiming the Zapatistas already proved my whole model.
u7: Sociocracy arrived at some similar forms from a very different history. It works with circles and consent. It distributes authority and links its levels together. That resemblance doesn't prove there's a universal formula. But it gives people building a community another serious system to study, so they don't have to invent their governance in the middle of their first dispute.
